collected: Real job ads collected manually from Seek, September 2026
headline: Not one of these 10 ads required a completed IT qualification.

terms.plain: Microsoft's system for managing who can log in to what. Used to be called Azure Active Directory. You'd use it to create and remove staff accounts.
The older, on-site version of the same thing - the database of users, computers and permissions in a company.
A logged request from a staff member or customer. You pick it up, fix it, and write down what you did. 'Level 1' tickets are the simple ones.
How difficult the problem is. Level 1 is password resets and printers. Level 2 is harder stuff. If you can't fix it, you 'escalate' it to someone more senior.
Passing a problem to someone more senior when you can't solve it. Ads treat knowing WHEN to escalate as a skill, not a failure.
A company that runs IT for other businesses. You'd support many different clients rather than one employer.
Software as a Service - software you use through a browser instead of installing it. Most workplace tools now.
Entry-level IT certificates. You study and sit an exam. Nine of these ten ads mention certifications, but only one actually requires you to have one.
Microsoft's beginner certificates for cloud, Microsoft 365 and security. Cheap, done online, and several employers here pay for them.
They need to know your visa lets you work the hours the job needs. Check your own conditions before you rule yourself out - student and graduate visas differ.
A background check you apply for and pay for. Takes days to weeks. One ad here needs it issued within 3 months and renewed every year.

terms.term: Working with Children Check (Blue Card in QLD)
terms.plain: Required for any job around under-18s. You apply through the state. Takes weeks, so start it before you apply, not after the interview.
Not-for-profits can pay part of your salary before tax, so you take home more. The Indie Education ad offers up to $15,900 plus $2,650 for meals.
A pay scale negotiated for the whole organisation. 'Level 3' tells you where you sit on it. The rate is fixed, so there's less to negotiate.
You take turns being contactable outside work hours in case something breaks. One ad here has it, one explicitly says they don't.
Split between office and home. Check the specific days - one ad here requires Monday, Tuesday and Thursday in the office.
Basic networking terms - how computers find each other and connect. Ads calling for 'networking fundamentals' mean these.
Text commands used to do admin tasks quickly instead of clicking. Listed as helpful-not-essential in the entry-level ads.

mustHave.note: Asked in the application questions of almost every ad. Know your own visa conditions before applying.
Every ad asks for this in some form. Several list it before any technical skill.
The one genuinely universal requirement across all ten ads.
The single most common technical requirement. Worth learning first if you're starting from zero.
Half the ads. Some also require your own car for travel to client sites.
Writing down what you did. Mentioned as a real requirement, not an afterthought.
Education and government employers. Takes days to weeks - start early.
Required where the workplace involves under-18s. Weeks to obtain.

niceToHave.note: Mentioned in 9 of 10 ads but required in only 1. Most employers here will pay for yours after you start.
Not one ad required a completed qualification. Every single one said 'or equivalent experience', 'or working towards one', or listed study as optional.

niceToHave.item: Networking beyond the basics (firewalls, routing, VLANs)
niceToHave.note: Consistently in the bonus list, not the essential list.
Listed as helpful, never required, even in the systems administration role.
One ad listed it as required; the rest treat it as a bonus.
Nice to have. Not having it doesn't stop you applying.
Fitness, education, telco. Explicitly 'desirable but not essential' where mentioned.

getReady.why: Only needed for education or youth-facing employers, but it's the longest lead time of anything here. Start it the moment you consider those roles.
One ad required it issued within the last 3 months. You apply and pay for it yourself.

getReady.time: Months if you don't have one
getReady.why: Half these ads want it. If you don't have an Australian licence, this shapes which jobs you can realistically target.
Several ads ask for these upfront. Message people now and ask permission rather than scrambling.
Cheap, online, and it appears in 9 of 10 ads. Not required anywhere, but it's the fastest way to look serious.

getReady.item: A cover letter addressing the selection criteria
getReady.why: Two ads asked for this specifically. It means writing a response to each requirement, not a general letter.

getReady.item: One story about a technical problem you solved
getReady.why: One ad asks for this directly, and it comes up in every interview. Say what broke, what you did, and what changed.
9 of 10 ads ask about work rights. Know your exact answer so you don't self-reject from a job you're allowed to do.
